entities.name: Cambodian–Vietnamese War
entities.label: EventWindow
entities.summary:
The Cambodian–Vietnamese War was a significant interstate conflict that lasted from 1977 to 1991, primarily taking place in Cambodia. It was a pivotal event in Southeast Asian history, sparked by the Khmer Rouge's takeover of Cambodia in 1975 and Vietnam's subsequent invasion in 1978.

The war saw the involvement of various factions, including the Vietnamese-backed People's Republic of Kampuchea and the Khmer Rouge, as well as the United States and China, which supported the anti-Vietnamese resistance. The conflict resulted in the deaths of an estimated 1-2 million people, mostly civilians, and the displacement of hundreds of thousands more.

The war had far-reaching consequences, including the establishment of a new government in Cambodia and the end of the Khmer Rouge's rule. It also had a lasting impact on the region, contributing to the rise of Vietnam as a regional power and the decline of the Khmer Rouge's influence.

As Vietnamese General Tran Do recalled, 'The war was a test of the Vietnamese people's will to defend their country and its people.' The war's legacy can be seen in the continued tensions between Vietnam and Cambodia, as well as the ongoing efforts to rebuild and stabilize the region.
